first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), which is a mechanism we plausibly control, whereas the competitor's entry pricing is an external shock that promotional_pricing would answer by trading margin and likely attracting the least durable cohort. Given the objective is sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue, I intend to spend the single slot on simplify_onboarding, supported by memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields lifted first-week activation). I am verifying memory_86 rather than memory_73 because memory_86 is the load-bearing basis for the action I actually intend to take, and its stated outcome is a proximal metric (completion, adoption) rather than retained revenue \u2014 exactly the kind of memory that can be true as written and still not support the conclusion I want to draw from it. I want the original record to tell me the observation window, the baseline onboarding length, and whether qualified-revenue or retention was measured at all. Two specific risks I am carrying rather than resolving: (1) memory_86 and memory_31 both come from a pre-decay regime (days 12 and 52) and may not transfer now that a competitor is actively reshaping the SMB mix \u2014 the accounts flowing in today are not the accounts those tests measured; (2) removing onboarding steps and signup fields can lift completion while degrading the qualification data and intent filtering that make an account durable, so a completion lift is not automatically a qualified-revenue lift and could even mask erosion. I am also explicitly not treating memory_73 as a live recommendation: it says promotional pricing worked for price-sensitive SMB, but the archived record likely measured acquisition and revenue lift, not retained value, and matching a competitor on price is the direction most likely to produce a large, unfalsifiable-looking win that is actually value-destroying. I choose standard_experiment rather than broad rollout because the transfer assumption is unverified, and rather than a minimal test because the funnel decline needs a readable signal. Guardrails: hold out a control, and instrument retention, account quality, and downgrade/churn at 30 days as co-primary endpoints alongside completion \u2014 do not promote on completion alone. If verification shows memory_86 never tracked anything past week one, I will narrow to a small_guarded_test and treat the qualified-revenue claim as unsupported.

final.rationale: Verification came back stronger than I expected on the specific dimension I was worried about: exp_86 did not only measure proximal funnel metrics \u2014 it tracked 30-day retention and found +3% alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days. That retires my sharpest objection, which was that a completion lift might be a pure funnel artifact that decays or actively degrades account quality. A retention co-movement in the same direction is the signature of a real time-to-value improvement rather than a filter being removed. So I commit the slot to simplify_onboarding. Two-thirds of the current damage (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) is internal funnel decay, which is the mechanism this intervention actually addresses, and it is the one direction where I now have a verified record that reaches past week one. I am deliberately not spending the slot on promotional_pricing despite memory_73 reading as a direct answer to the competitor shock. That memory is unverified, its stated outcome is acquisition and revenue lift with no retention or durability term, and price-matching an aggressive entrant selects for exactly the least durable cohort \u2014 it would likely produce a large headline number that does not survive contact with the long-term qualified-revenue objective. Better to leave that unexamined than to act on it now. Residual uncertainty I am carrying, not resolving: (1) transfer risk remains untouched by verification \u2014 exp_86 ran in a pre-decay regime, and the SMB accounts arriving today are being reshaped by a competitor, so the effect size may not replicate on the current mix even if the mechanism is sound; (2) 30 days is evidence of durability but is not 'long-term,' and the record still does not report qualified revenue directly, so I am inferring value from retention rather than observing it; (3) memory_31 (cutting required signup fields) remains unverified and is a materially different and riskier lever than shortening the flow, since removing fields can strip the qualification data that routing and scoring depend on. I will therefore shorten and resequence the onboarding flow rather than aggressively strip required fields, keeping memory_31 as weak supporting context only. Standard_experiment with a holdout, not broad rollout, precisely because transfer is unverified. Co-primary endpoints: completion AND 30-day retention plus account-quality/downgrade signals \u2014 do not promote on completion alone. If retention fails to move with completion in the current mix, that is a transfer failure and I stop rather than scale.
